working: In a cyclic quadrilateral opposite angles are supplementary: \(A+C=\pi\) and \(B+D=\pi\), so \(\cos C=-\cos A\) and \(\cos D=-\cos B\); the sum telescopes to 0. Numeric check with \(A=80^\circ,C=100^\circ,B=70^\circ,D=110^\circ\): \(0.1736-0.1736+0.3420-0.3420=0\).

\(\cos 40^\circ+\cos 80^\circ=2\cos 60^\circ\cos 20^\circ=\cos 20^\circ\), and \(\cos 160^\circ=-\cos 20^\circ\), so those three cancel; \(\cos 240^\circ=-\tfrac12\). Numeric: \(0.766+0.1736-0.9397-0.5=-0.5\).

\(\pi/12=15^\circ\) and \(5\pi/12=75^\circ\) are complementary, so \(\cos^2 15^\circ+\cos^2 75^\circ=\cos^2 15^\circ+\sin^2 15^\circ=1\); adding \(\cos^2 45^\circ=\tfrac12\) gives \(\tfrac32\). Numeric: \(0.9330+0.5+0.0670=1.5\).

\(2\sin\frac{A}{2}\sin\frac{5A}{2}=\cos 2A-\cos 3A\), so the expression is \(16(\cos 2A-\cos 3A)\). With \(\cos A=\tfrac34\): \(\cos 2A=2(9/16)-1=1/8\) and \(\cos 3A=4(27/64)-3(3/4)=27/16-36/16=-9/16\). Difference \(=2/16+9/16=11/16\), times 16 gives 11.

For each angle \((\sec\theta+\tan\theta)(\sec\theta-\tan\theta)=\sec^2\theta-\tan^2\theta=1\), so the required product is the reciprocal of the given one: \(1/(\tan\alpha\tan\beta\tan\gamma)=\cot\alpha\cot\beta\cot\gamma\).

GM condition: \(\sin^2\beta=\sin\alpha\cos\alpha\). Then \(\cos 2\beta=1-2\sin^2\beta=1-2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha=1-\sin 2\alpha\). Option A: \(2\sin^2(\pi/4-\alpha)=1-\cos(\pi/2-2\alpha)=1-\sin 2\alpha\). Numeric check \(\alpha=30^\circ\): \(\sin^2\beta=0.4330\Rightarrow\cos2\beta=1-0.8660=0.1340\); \(2\sin^2 15^\circ=0.1340\).

In a triangle \(\tan\frac{A}{2}\tan\frac{B}{2}+\tan\frac{B}{2}\tan\frac{C}{2}+\tan\frac{C}{2}\tan\frac{A}{2}=1\). Substituting: \(\frac13\cdot\frac23+\tan\frac{C}{2}\left(\frac23+\frac13\right)=1\Rightarrow \frac29+\tan\frac{C}{2}=1\Rightarrow \tan\frac{C}{2}=\frac79\). Check: \(A/2=18.435^\circ, B/2=33.690^\circ\Rightarrow C/2=90-52.125=37.875^\circ\), \(\tan 37.875^\circ=0.7778=7/9\).

working: Adding 1 to each term keeps the AP: \(\frac{a+b+c}{b+c},\frac{a+b+c}{c+a},\frac{a+b+c}{a+b}\) in AP, so \(\frac{1}{b+c},\frac{1}{c+a},\frac{1}{a+b}\) are in AP. Then \(2(b+c)(a+b)=(c+a)(a+2b+c)\) reduces to \(2b^2=a^2+c^2\), i.e. \(a^2,b^2,c^2\) in AP. Numeric check with \(a=1,b=5,c=7\) (\(1,25,49\) in AP): \(\frac1{12},\frac58,\frac76\) have common difference \(\frac{13}{24}\) — confirmed; note \(1,5,7\) is not an AP/GP, ruling out A, B and D.

\(\sin^{-1}u\) needs \(-1\le u\le 1\); with \(u=5x\) this gives \(-\tfrac15\le x\le\tfrac15\), a CLOSED interval (the endpoints \(x=\pm 1/5\) give \(\sin^{-1}(\pm1)=\pm\pi/2\), which is defined), so \([-1/5,1/5]\) not the open interval of option A.

Denominator \(x^2+x-6=(x+3)(x-2)\) vanishes at \(x=2\) and \(x=-3\), so the domain is \(R\setminus\{2,-3\}\). (The numerator \((x-1)(x-2)\) also vanishes at \(x=2\), but a \(0/0\) point is still excluded from the domain — the function is simply undefined there.)

\(\sin 2x\) has period \(2\pi/2=\pi\); taking the modulus folds the negative half onto the positive half and halves the period, giving \(\pi/2\). Check: \(|\sin 2(x+\pi/2)|=|\sin(2x+\pi)|=|-\sin 2x|=|\sin 2x|\), and no smaller value works since \(|\sin 2x|=0\) exactly at multiples of \(\pi/2\).

\(\vec a\cdot\vec b=0\Rightarrow\) perpendicular. \(\cos 60^\circ=\frac{(\vec a+\vec b)\cdot\vec a}{|\vec a+\vec b||\vec a|}=\frac{|\vec a|}{|\vec a+\vec b|}=\tfrac12\Rightarrow|\vec a+\vec b|=2|\vec a|\). Since \(|\vec a+\vec b|^2=|\vec a|^2+|\vec b|^2\), we get \(|\vec b|^2=3|\vec a|^2\), i.e. \(|\vec b|=\sqrt3|\vec a|\), which is option D (\(\sqrt3|\vec a|=|\vec b|\)). Check \(\vec a=(1,0),\vec b=(0,\sqrt3)\): \(\vec a+\vec b=(1,\sqrt3)\) makes \(60^\circ\) with the x-axis. Option C is the reversed relation.
Independence \(\Rightarrow \mathrm{cov}(x,y)=0\Rightarrow r=0\), and \(b_{yx}=\mathrm{cov}(x,y)/\sigma_x^2=r\sigma_y/\sigma_x=0\).

Equal distances each way, so average speed is the harmonic mean: \(\frac{2\cdot 12\cdot 14}{12+14}=\frac{336}{26}=\frac{168}{13}=12\frac{12}{13}\) km/h. Sanity check with \(d=84\) km: times \(7\) h and \(6\) h, total \(168/13\) km/h — matches, and it lies between 12 and 14 as it must.
subtopic: Harmonic Progressions and the Three Means
notes: Option (C) is printed as "11 km//h" — a stray doubled slash for "11 km/h". Cosmetic only; (C) is a distractor either way (11 lies outside [12,14] and cannot be an average of the two speeds).

working: With \(C=90^\circ\), \(\tan\frac{B}{2}=\frac{\sin B}{1+\cos B}=\frac{b/c}{1+a/c}=\frac{b}{c+a}\); since \(b^2=c^2-a^2=(c-a)(c+a)\), this equals \(\sqrt{\frac{c-a}{c+a}}\). Numeric check on the 3-4-5 triangle (\(a=3,b=4,c=5\)): \(\tan(B/2)=\frac{4/5}{8/5}=\tfrac12\) and \(\sqrt{2/8}=\tfrac12\). Option B is negative under the radical (\(a<c\) always), option C is the reciprocal.

working: By the sine rule, \(\frac{\cos C+\cos A}{c+a}=\frac{2\cos\frac{A+C}{2}\cos\frac{A-C}{2}}{2R\cdot 2\sin\frac{A+C}{2}\cos\frac{A-C}{2}}=\frac{\cot\frac{A+C}{2}}{2R}=\frac{\tan\frac{B}{2}}{2R}\), while \(\frac{1-\cos B}{b}=\frac{1-\cos B}{2R\sin B}=\frac{\tan\frac{B}{2}}{2R}\); hence the expression \(=\frac{1}{b}\). Verified numerically on two triangles: \((3,4,5)\) gives \(\frac{4/5}{8}+\frac{3/5}{4}=\tfrac14=\tfrac1b\), and \((2,3,4)\) gives \(\frac{5/8}{6}+\frac{11/16}{3}=\tfrac13=\tfrac1b\) — both single out \(1/b\) over \(1/a\) and \(1/c\).

working: The terms are \(\frac85,\frac{12}5,\frac{16}5,\frac{20}5,\frac{24}5,\dots\), i.e. \(t_k=\frac{4(k+1)}5\). Sum of squares of the first 10: \(\frac{16}{25}\sum_{k=1}^{10}(k+1)^2=\frac{16}{25}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{11}k^2-1\right)=\frac{16}{25}(506-1)=\frac{16}{25}\cdot 505=\frac{16}{5}\cdot 101=323.2\). Comparing with \(\frac{16}{5}m\) gives \(m=101\).
